newsitem.title: USA: Arco seeks extra $500 million for Alaska projects.
newsitem.headline: Arco seeks extra $500 million for Alaska projects.

text.p: Atlantic Richfield plans to spend an additional $500 million on Alaska capital projects in the next five years, on top of $1.2 billion already slated for 1997-2001, the head of the copmany's Alaska division said on Wednesday.
Arco Alaska President Ken Thompson said the parent company's bullishness on Alaska reflected an improved business climate in the state and the company's technological and economic advances.

"The board is looking for new growth within Arco and likes what they see in Alaska, with the better business environment, the lower cost structure and these technological improvements," Thompson said in a joint news conference with Alaska Gov. Tony Knowles.
Arco Chairman Mike Bowlin and other senior officials have approved the plan for increased Alaska spending and will submit it to the board of directors in January, Thompson said.
The announcement followed a trip by Knowles Monday to Arco's California headquarters.
If the board approved the additional $500 million, Thompson said Arco Alaska would spend the resulting total $1.7 billion on the following:
- about $475 million over the next five years for exploration and delineation drilling
- about $400 million to develop Arco's share of the new Alpine prospect east of the Kuparuk field.
- $300 million on enhanced recovery and new drilling at the supergiant Prudhoe Bay field
- $275 million for enhanced recovery at the Kuparuk field
- $120 million on producing heavy oil at the West Sak field and about $100 million on miscellaneous projects.
Some of the spending plans depended on approval from Arco's North Slope partners, he said.

Arco's exploration plans include additional drilling on leases near the Alpine discovery, he said. Targeted are leases held by Arco's Alpine partners, Anadarko Petroleum and Union Texas Petroleum, he said.

The Alpine accumulation, 250 million to 300 million recoverable barrels, was unveiled in October. The field is located in the Colville River delta, just over the western border of the 23 million acre National Petroleum Reserve-Alaska.

Arco Alaska plans seismic tests in the petroleum reserve and, if the area is opened to drilling, may seek new funds for further exploration there, Thompson said. "At this point, I'd just say it's a prospective area of interest to industry."
The federally owned petroleum reserve was the site of oil and gas exploration -- and some discoveries -- between the 1940s and 1980s.

It was bypassed for better North Slope prospects, but modern technology could unlock commercial petroleum quantities in the reserve, representatives of the U.S. Interior Department and oil industry have suggested.
Knowles, who held a daylong meeting with Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt in Seattle Tuesday, expressed hopes for new oil development in the reserve.

"Because of the new technology, the lower cost and the good business climate, industry is interested in looking at it," said Knowles, a Democrat. "I think this is something that the federal government can do now to continue the very positive exploration and production in Alaska."
